key_insight: LLM confidence is driven by two competing biases: a choice-supportive bias that boosts confidence in initial answers, and a systematic overweighting of contradictory advice that produces deviations from Bayesian-optimal updating, explaining both overconfidence and underconfidence.
problem_solved: Explains why large language models show inconsistent confidence calibration and how distinct psychological-style biases (choice-support and advice overweighting) cause systematic departures from normative Bayesian belief updates.
method: Controlled "decision + advice" experiments with LLMs: record initial answer and confidence, present conflicting advice, then measure updated confidence and choice.
Quantitative comparison of observed updates to Bayesian-optimal updates to identify systematic deviations and quantify bias direction/magnitude.
Cross-model and ablation analyses to verify robustness of biases across architectures and settings.
impact: Clarifies mechanistic sources of miscalibration in LLMs, informing better confidence estimation, safer deployment, and targeted interventions (e.g., calibration methods or prompt designs) to reduce harmful over- or under-confidence.
visual_elements: Timeline/flow diagram: initial choice → contradictory advice → updated confidence (showing movement direction)
Bar/violin plot: magnitude and sign of confidence change vs. Bayesian-predicted update (overweighting vs underweighting)
Schematic 'tug-of-war' icon: two opposing arrows representing choice-supportive bias and advice-overweighting bias acting on confidence
Calibration curve or reliability diagram: model confidence vs. actual accuracy before and after advice
paper_title: Competing Biases underlie Overconfidence and Underconfidence in LLMs
paper_authors: Dharshan Kumaran, Stephen M. Fleming, Larisa Markeeva, Joe Heyward, Andrea Banino
